chapters.title: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude: The Law of Self-Sabotage

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter on self-sabotage stays useful because it names a pattern people often feel before they can explain it. This law argues that attitude filters what people notice, attempt, and persist with, so a constricted attitude quietly sabotages options that an expansive attitude can still use. Self-sabotage happens because the mind keeps confirming the attitude it is already carrying. If you expect humiliation, you will notice slights. If you expect futility, you will underinvest early. In that sense, attitude shapes circumstance indirectly by shaping perception, confidence, and persistence. The practical move is to catch the interpretive habit before it hardens into destiny. Reframe setbacks, widen the range of possible responses, and use the inner freedom to choose your stance even where the external situation is still difficult. Attitude widens response space; it does not erase reality. That softer honesty is already a practical advantage.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter on self-sabotage matters because it lowers the drama and names the pattern more carefully than everyday language usually does. Two people can walk through the same setback and emerge in radically different worlds because one treats the event as proof of closure while the other treats it as material that can still be worked with. Greene describes attitude as a lens rather than a mood sticker. A constricted attitude searches for insult, danger, futility, and helplessness. An expansive attitude looks for room to maneuver, lessons, and next moves. The difference is practical before it is inspirational. Self-sabotage happens because the mind keeps confirming the attitude it is already carrying. If you expect humiliation, you will notice slights. If you expect futility, you will underinvest early.
